'''Frederick Ludwig Hoffman''' (May 2, 1865 – February 23, 1946) was an American [[statistician]] known for his work on health and demographic statistics. He is also notable for his promotion of [[scientific racism]], and is a vocal opponent of government backed health insurance and social welfare.<ref>{{Cite magazine |url=https://magazine.amstat.org/blog/2018/10/29/sih-hoffman/ |title=Frederick L. Hoffman (1865–1946) |first=Francis J. Jr. |last=Rigney |magazine=[[Amstat News]] |date=2018-10-29 |access-date=2023-07-04}}</ref><ref>Hoffman B. Scientific Racism, Insurance, and Opposition to the Welfare State: Frederick L. Hoffman’s Transatlantic Journey. ''The Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era''. 2003;2(2):150-190. doi:10.1017/S1537781400002450</ref>

==Biography==
Hoffman was born ''Friedrich Ludwig Hoffmann'' in [[Varel]] in the [[Grand Duchy of Oldenburg]] on May 2, 1865 the son of the merchant Augustus Franziskus Hoffmann and his wife Antonette.<ref name=Sypher>{{Cite journal |url=http://www.cosmosclub.org/journals/2000/sypher.html|title=The Rediscovered Prophet: Frederick L. Hoffman (1865-1946) |first=Francis J. |last=Sypher |journal=Cosmos 2000 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180715093756/http://www.cosmosclub.org/journals/2000/sypher.html |archive-date=2018-07-15 |url-status=dead |access-date=2023-07-04}}</ref><ref name=CyclopediaNJ>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/biographicalcycl00bige/page/147/mode/1up |title=The Biographical Cyclopedia of New Jersey |editor1-first=Samuel F. |editor1-last=Bigelow |editor1-link=Samuel Fowler Bigelow |editor2-first=George J. |editor2-last=Hagar |publisher=National Americana Society |place=New York City |pages=147–149 |date=1909 |access-date=2023-07-04 |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> His father died when Frederick was 11 years old. He was educated in the common and private schools in Germany. His school days, marked by failures, ended in 1880 without a degree. At the request of his single mother, who was now living in difficult financial circumstances, Frederick began a four-year commercial apprenticeship with various merchants in north-west Germany. The apprenticeship ended in 1884 also without a degree. Since Frederick saw no further professional and personal future for himself in Germany, he emigrated to the United States at the end of 1884.<ref>On Hoffman's childhood and youth in Varel and the surrounding area see: Hans Sauer: ''From school dropout to recognized publicist, Friedrich Ludwig Hoffmann - a biographical sketch'', in: Dirk Oltmanns (Ed.), ''Emigration from the Oldenburg Land to the USA. Individual Fates with Backgrounds, Letters and Photos'', Oldenburg (Germany) 2023, p. 90-105 (contact: www.hollwege.com).</ref> He became statistician for the [[Prudential Insurance Company of America]] in 1891. Hoffman was a racist against African Americans in his studies of incarceration. He was employed as statistician by many organizations and did research in ethnology and kindred subjects. He also served as [[President of the American Statistical Association]] in 1911.

Hoffman's first book, ''The Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro'' (1896), characterized [[African American]]s as exceptionally disease-prone. The work was motivated by a concern about issues of race,{{cn|date=July 2023}} and also the need of insurance companies to justify the higher [[life insurance]] premiums charged to African Americans.{{cn|date=July 2023}} An 1897 critique of this work by [[Kelly Miller (scientist)|Kelly Miller]] in occasional papers of the American Negro Academy of Washington, D.C., pointed out sampling problems with the [[1890 United States census|1890 census]], which was the statistical basis of the work, and that there were insufficient adjustments for environmental factors.{{cn|date=July 2023}} Hoffman found, contrary to common rhetoric at the time, that the population of African Americans was not increasing at a substantially more rapid pace than the White population.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Dawson |first=Miles Menander |date=1896 |title=Review of Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2276196 |journal=Publications of the American Statistical Association |volume=5 |issue=35/36 |pages=142–148 |doi=10.2307/2276196 |issn=1522-5437|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=DuBois |first=W. E. Burghardt |date=1897 |title=Review of Race Traits and Tendencies of the American Negro |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1009520 |journal=The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science |volume=9 |pages=127–133 |issn=0002-7162}}</ref> He found that while African Americans had a higher birth rate, they had an even higher mortality rate, which meant that the population of Whites increased at a higher pace than African Americans.<ref name=":0" /> 

He married Ella G. Hay on July 15, 1891, and they had seven children.<ref name=CyclopediaNJ/>

He died in [[San Diego]], California on February 23, 1946.<ref name=Sypher/><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-boston-globe-frederick-l-hoffman/127599884/ |title=Frederick L. Hoffman |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |place=San Diego, California |agency=AP |page=15 |date=1946-02-24 |publication-date=1946-02-25 |access-date=2023-07-04 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref> He was buried at [[Greenwood Memorial Park (San Diego)|Greenwood Memorial Park]].<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-los-angeles-times/19813464/ |title=Dr. Frederick Hoffman, Cancer Authority, Dies |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |page=12 |place=San Diego |date=1946-02-24 |publication-date=1946-02-25 |access-date=2023-07-04 |via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

A collection of his papers are held at the [[National Library of Medicine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://findingaids.nlm.nih.gov/repositories/ammp/resources/holman|title=Emile Holman Papers 1909-1976|publisher=National Library of Medicine}}</ref>
